html:
Gwich'in Nành, "the land of the Gwich'in", covers northeastern Alaska, the northern Yukon and the Mackenzie Delta. The Gwich'in are the most northerly Athabaskan people, living along the Yukon, Porcupine and Peel rivers, south of the Inupiat of the Arctic coast.

Their life has long centred on the Porcupine caribou herd, which they hunted with fences and corrals as it migrated, and on fish from the rivers. Bands such as the Vuntut Gwitchin of Old Crow and the Tetlit Gwich'in of the Peel are part of the nation.

The Hudson's Bay Company built Fort Yukon in 1847 inside Russian territory, and Anglican missionaries followed in the 1860s, translating the Bible into Gwich'in. Today the Gwich'in are divided by the Alaska and Canada border. Since the 1980s they have led the fight against oil drilling on the caribou calving grounds in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
